video_title: Stephanie Pomboy: 2027 Is Going To Be "Brutal In A Way We Haven't Experienced"
gist: Stephanie Pomboy argues October's hot CPI is stale data and the Fed tightening scare will reverse as a non-discretionary-spending-dominated, debt-funded consumer weakens into 2027; she sees state-level anti-business/anti-data-center regulation, deteriorating credit quality, and an economy dependent on the stock market setting up a brutal bear market that forces outright QE, favoring gold, hard assets and short-duration Treasuries.

themes.theme: Hot CPI is stale; disinflation ahead

insights.claim: October CPI printed 0.4% month-over-month vs 0.3% expected, pushing December quarter-point Fed hike odds to ~99% and lifting 2027 hike odds, which hit stocks, precious metals and Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Rate-sensitive assets are trading tick-by-tick on hike odds; a reversal in hike expectations is the swing factor for metals and crypto.

insights.claim: Fed governor Waller said before the print that he favored a hike unless CPI came in at 0.3%; the 0.4% print effectively locked in tightening expectations.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Fed speakers are explicitly data-contingent, so each monthly print can move front-end pricing sharply.

insights.claim: Stephanie Pomboy views the hot CPI as rearview-mirror data and expects the market's fear of Fed tightening to flip entirely the other way in reasonably short order because post-election policy is not growth-positive.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Positions betting on a sustained hiking cycle (short front-end, short metals) are vulnerable to a reversal once stale data rolls off.

insights.claim: The post-election drop in long-dated yields was mostly driven by falling oil prices on hopes of an Iran resolution; roughly two-thirds of the move was lower inflation expectations and one-third real yields.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: The long-end rally rests on oil; if oil rebounds, the inflation-expectation component of the rally unwinds.

insights.claim: Producer prices (PPI) are now rising faster than consumer prices (CPI) by the largest gap since COVID, implying a real margin squeeze for companies unable to pass costs on.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Watch consumer-facing company margins; the PPI-CPI gap signals earnings pressure hidden by AI-inflated headline earnings.
insights.quote: it is now outstripping the CPI by the largest amount since COVID

insights.claim: Headline S&P earnings are being inflated by the AI boom and circular financing, masking weaker positions at consumer-facing companies, which are already overrepresented in bankruptcy filings.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Index-level earnings strength may not reflect consumer discretionary fundamentals; be selective/underweight there.

insights.claim: Shelter accounted for over 30% of October's monthly CPI gain despite rents nationally disinflating or deflating, possibly due to utilities, insurance costs, and heavy CPI weighting of urban centers like Manhattan and Boston.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Shelter's CPI contribution may not track national rent declines, so don't assume rent deflation quickly drags CPI lower.

insights.claim: CPI shelter lags home prices and rents by roughly 12-18 months because it is computed via owner's equivalent rent, so monthly shelter moves say little about current housing conditions.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Use private-sector rent and price data rather than CPI shelter to gauge real-time housing inflation.

insights.claim: Pomboy expects the Fed may deliver another 25bp in December if data continues, but she does not expect a material tightening cycle.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Pricing of an extended 2027 hiking path is likely to be priced out, favoring the front end of the curve.
insights.quote: this is not going to be a material tightening cycle

insights.claim: A resolution with Iran (e.g., an MOU) pushing oil into the high $60s could remove the case for a December rate hike, and October CPI does not yet reflect the recent oil decline.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Oil is the key variable for near-term Fed decisions; geopolitical headlines on Iran can swing rate and metals trades.

insights.claim: Of $113 billion in nominal consumer spending growth in September, $46 billion was gasoline and energy goods, $20 billion transportation and $18 billion housing and utilities; Pomboy calculates 96% was non-discretionary, leaving only about $4 billion by choice.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Headline spending strength is illusory; discretionary retailers and services face weak real demand.
insights.quote: I calculated that 96% of the consumer spending in the month of September was non-discretionary stuff

insights.claim: Recreation services spending posted roughly the third-largest percentage decline in its history dating back to 1960 in September's PCE report.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Leisure and experiences spending is cracking; watch travel/entertainment names for demand weakness.

insights.claim: Investors misread consumer strength because nominal spending and retail sales are flattered by inflation rather than reflecting more units purchased.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Deflate spending data by prices and examine composition before concluding the consumer is healthy.

insights.claim: Consumers have shifted funding from COVID stimulus to credit cards, then to home equity lines of credit, and to buy now pay later, signaling an unhealthy consumer funding spending with debt.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Rising consumer leverage raises credit-loss risk for card issuers, HELOC lenders and BNPL providers.

insights.claim: Pomboy describes buy now pay later as resembling a Ponzi scheme that depends on new customer sign-ups to cover non-paying borrowers, and expects a reckoning when the can can no longer be kicked.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: BNPL providers are exposed to a growth stall that would expose defaults.
insights.quote: it feels to me like it's the classic Ponzi scheme

insights.claim: Holiday spending will likely hold up through year-end funded by credit, but Pomboy expects consumer spending to tighten sharply in early 2027.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Q4 retail data may look fine; the consumer-driven slowdown is a Q1 2027 story.

insights.claim: JP Morgan data showing customers withdrawing from brokerage accounts to fund living expenses indicates stress has moved up the income spectrum, since low-end consumers don't have brokerage accounts.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Affordability stress is broader than the low-income cohort, threatening the middle/upper-middle consumer.
insights.quote: the low-end consumer hardly has a bank account. He sure as hell doesn't have a brokerage account.

insights.claim: Pomboy's simple 'misery index' of mortgage rate plus gasoline price exceeded 12 and rose above its Biden-era COVID-inflation peak, which she says made affordability the decisive election issue.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: A simple affordability gauge for tracking consumer pain and political pressure.
insights.quote: adding the mortgage rate to the gasoline price. And I just called it the misery index.

insights.claim: Affordability relief requires either wage growth that outpaces prices, which hasn't happened, or real goods-and-services disinflation, which would only come with a massive economic slowdown.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: No painless path to affordability; expect either persistent squeeze or recession.

themes.theme: State-level politics and AI data centers

insights.claim: Pomboy argues the post-election view that Washington gridlock is good is a gross misapprehension because newly elected state governors with anti-business and anti-fossil-fuel agendas can impose regulation easily.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Political risk for growth has shifted to the state level; monitor state regulation rather than Congress.
insights.quote: gridlock is good because you know now Washington can do no harm is a gross misapprehension

insights.claim: Federal deregulation under Trump can be re-erected at the state level, and AI data centers are the clearest target given bipartisan pushback.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: State permitting and regulatory risk could slow AI data-center build-outs and the capex they drive.
insights.quote: think about how much regulation Trump has removed at the federal level that can then be reerected essentially at the state level

insights.claim: Adam Taggart notes the market sell-off the Thursday after the election was attributed to Democrats winning on largely anti-AI/data-center platforms at the state level, and that a 20-30% slower AI rollout would force markets to ratchet down asset prices.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: AI-capex-dependent equities carry regulatory downside not yet fully priced.

insights.claim: Any state-level slowdown in economic activity feeds directly into a larger federal deficit via higher social welfare spending and lower tax revenue, undermining the 'gridlock caps the deficit' real-yield rally.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Bond bulls counting on fiscal restraint may be wrong; deficits can widen without new federal legislation.

insights.claim: Pomboy expects complete gridlock in Washington is more likely than Republicans breaking ranks to pass a Democratic affordability agenda over Trump's veto.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Little federal policy change expected; focus on state-level and monetary drivers.

insights.claim: Junk borrowers are refinancing debt that carried ~4% coupons at yields over 8%, roughly doubling debt service costs for smaller, riskier companies.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Refinancing walls make weaker high-yield issuers vulnerable if earnings growth slows.
insights.quote: I'm looking at a junk yield here over 8% where those companies are refinancing paper that was carrying a 4%

insights.claim: Credit stress becomes acute when earnings growth slows while rates stay high; corporate profits up 50%+ in Q1 and 30%+ in Q2 have so far covered the higher debt costs.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Watch for decelerating earnings plus sticky yields as the trigger for credit spread blowouts.

insights.claim: Lending risk has been passed like a hot potato between banks and private credit, and Pomboy says she wouldn't touch leveraged/private lending with a 10-foot pole.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Avoid private credit and leveraged loan exposure; the question is when, not if, it blows up.
insights.quote: I wouldn't touch any of this stuff with a 10-ft pole

insights.claim: 56% of investment-grade debt is now BBB-rated versus about a third before the 2007 crisis, plus leveraged loans and unrated private credit, meaning debt quality is much lower than pre-GFC.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: A downturn could trigger mass fallen-angel downgrades; IG credit is riskier than ratings suggest.
insights.quote: today 56% of the investment grade is triple B rated

insights.claim: CFTC data show speculators remain as short the 10-year as before even as yields fell from about 5.3% to below 5%; the rally is driven by retail money leaving equities for Treasuries, not short covering.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: A large unrecovered spec short is fuel for a further 10-year rally in a full risk-off event.
insights.quote: There's been no capitulation by speculators.

insights.claim: Pomboy does not believe the peak in long rates is in; the 10-year might rally to ~4.5% but she expects substantially higher long yields three years out and prefers the front end of the curve.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Avoid long duration; use short-dated Treasuries, potentially adding after this week's data once hike fears fade.

insights.claim: Pomboy frames bonds as being in a secular bear market punctuated by vicious cyclical rallies driven by risk-off episodes or monetary intervention, making the front end preferable to sticking out on duration.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Trade duration rallies sparingly; core fixed income should be short duration.
insights.quote: we're in a secular bear market for bonds that will have within it some vicious cyclical rallies

themes.theme: Fed balance sheet and return of QE

insights.claim: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, a longtime critic of QE, is running about $40 billion a month of 'non-QE QE' and deferred balance-sheet answers to a task force report due around end of Q1.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: The Fed's balance sheet is already expanding despite rhetoric; watch it rather than the funds rate.
insights.quote: nothing is more expensive than free money

insights.claim: Pomboy expects non-QE QE in T-bills to become outright QE across the maturity spectrum, possibly in monster fashion, making the story about the currency.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Outright QE would debase the dollar, favoring hard assets over nominal bonds.
insights.quote: it's just a matter of time before non-QE QE becomes just outright QE

insights.claim: Pomboy says the market should focus on the Fed's balance sheet rather than the fed funds rate, since moving the policy rate has had precious little impact in recent cycles.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Balance-sheet signals are the better lead indicator for liquidity and asset prices.

insights.claim: The current setup resembles 2018, when the Fed tightened despite Trump's pressure until markets broke and forced the Fed's hand; Pomboy agrees with Jim Carson's call for an early-Q1 2027 market plunge prompting Fed intervention.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Position for a Q1 2027 risk-off event and a subsequent Fed pivot.

insights.claim: In a QE-driven rescue, investors should own precious metals and hard assets rather than the 10-year, because dollar purchasing power will be eviscerated.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Hedge intervention scenarios with hard assets, not long Treasuries.

insights.claim: Pomboy argues basically the entire economy rests on the stock market: AI companies now fund capex through equity issuance and circular financing, top-cohort consumers spend off wealth effects, and governments depend on capital gains taxes.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: An equity bear market would hit GDP far more than consensus assumes; reflexive risk to the whole economy.
insights.quote: basically the entire economy is resting on the stock market

insights.claim: State and local pensions remain $3-4 trillion underfunded even with markets near all-time highs, so a bear market would force spending cuts and tax hikes.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: State and local fiscal austerity would amplify any downturn; munis and state-dependent sectors at risk.

insights.claim: After the 2008-09 crisis, the state and local sector was a drag on GDP for four years; Pomboy says today's bubble and leverage are much larger.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Expect a prolonged fiscal drag after the next bear market, not a quick V.
insights.quote: it took the state and local sector of the economy four years before it started before it stopped being a drag on GDP

insights.claim: Adam Taggart argues the top 10-15% of households prop up average spending via asset gains, so a bear market would create a negative wealth effect that removes a large chunk of retail spending.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Luxury and high-end discretionary spending is highly exposed to equity drawdowns.

insights.claim: Pomboy rejects the idea that a bear market would be healthy cleansing, warning it would be brutal in a way not previously experienced and would force Fed balance-sheet re-expansion.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Bargain-hunting dry powder will find opportunity, but in a deeply unpleasant macro and social backdrop.
insights.quote: It's going to be brutal in a way that we haven't experienced.

insights.claim: Pomboy believes the CPI-driven precious metals sell-off is the worst of it and does not expect gold to revisit its prior ~$3,800 low, as the macro case for gold strengthened post-election and China keeps buying hand over fist.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: She views metals weakness as a buying opportunity driven by a misread of inflation and Fed tightening.
insights.quote: I think the macro case for gold just got so much stronger.

insights.claim: The Jensen Huang Chinese-spy affair exposes underappreciated key-person risks for Nvidia, including a potential investigation, CEO ouster, or divorce-driven share sales.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Concentration in Nvidia carries idiosyncratic governance/headline risk beyond fundamentals.

insights.claim: Pomboy's positioning remains precious metals, short-term Treasuries for dry powder, and selective energy and hard assets, and her one-word 2027 outlook is 'buckle up'.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: A defensive, hard-asset, short-duration template for a volatile 2027.
